p10.caption: Gol Stave Church, Norsk Folkemuseum
p10.story: I love the colour black, and that's a big part of why I liked looking at these churches.
p10.fact: It's around 800 years old. It was built in Gol, in Hallingdal, around 1200, and moved here and rebuilt in the 1880s.

p101.story: The drive back to the hytte from the kayaking and the Viking village. It rounded off something I was proud of: Norway was the first country outside India where I'd driven, and on the other side of the road.

p103.caption: Taj Mahal
p103.fact: Shah Jahan built it for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. The four minarets lean very slightly outwards, so that in an earthquake they'd fall away from the tomb.

p12.story: The end of the Oslo part of the trip. I swam (or at least tried to float) in open water for the first time in a very long time, in the Oslofjord. Then we grilled sausages on a disposable grill, and that was my first Norwegian hot dog.

p13.caption: Vigeland Park
p13.story:
I had never seen anything like Vigeland Park. Gustav Vigeland filled it with more than two hundred sculptures of people, and to be honest, I couldn't make sense of most of them.

But I don't think that's the point. It's less about working out what each one means and more about what it makes you feel. This one, two people holding on to each other, felt personal. I love how much intensity Vigeland put into that embrace.

p135.caption: Albert Hall Museum
p135.fact: Jaipur's oldest museum, and one of the few places in India where you can see a real Egyptian mummy.

p136.caption: Kulhad chai in the Pink City

p14.caption: The Wheel of Life
p14.story: At the far end of the park is the Wheel of Life, a ring of bodies holding on to one another. It was intriguing to look at. These sculptures feel different when you're standing in front of them than when you see them in print.

p143.caption: Victoria Memorial
p143.fact: Finished in 1921 and built from the same white Makrana marble as the Taj Mahal.

p145.caption: A Kolkata yellow taxi
p145.fact: The Hindustan Ambassador stopped being made in 2014, but in Kolkata the yellow ones are still everywhere. For now.

p146.caption: Howrah Bridge
p146.fact: Opened in 1943 and held together entirely by rivets: there isn't a single nut or bolt in it.

p156.caption: Kotor's cats
p156.fact: Kotor is famous for its cats: they wander the old town freely, and there's even a cats museum.

p162.caption: The city walls
p162.fact: The walls climb around 4.5 km up the mountain behind the old town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

p20.caption: The Adiyogi
p20.fact: At 34 metres, it's recognised by Guinness as the largest bust sculpture in the world.

p21.caption: Leadenhall Market
p21.fact: Look familiar? It stood in for Diagon Alley in the first Harry Potter film.

p22.fact: That little red and white lighthouse at the foot of the cliffs has been standing there since 1902.

p31.caption: The Lady Chapel, Westminster Abbey
p31.fact: The banners belong to the Knights of the Order of the Bath; this is their chapel.

p38.caption: Eilean Donan
p38.fact: It sat in ruins for almost 200 years before being rebuilt in the early 1900s, so it's younger than it looks.

p45.caption: Glenfinnan Viaduct
p45.fact: Yes, it's the Harry Potter one: the Hogwarts Express crosses it in the films. Back in 1901 it was also one of the first big structures built from mass concrete.

p46.caption: The Radcliffe Camera
p46.fact: Finished in 1749, it was the first circular library in England, and it's still a reading room today.

p57.fact: The smaller bluestones were hauled here from the Preseli Hills in Wales, about 150 miles away. Nobody's entirely sure how.

p60.story: What caught my eye was the contrast: an old building and a modern one side by side, sharing the same red.

p61.caption: Akershus Fortress
p61.fact: Building started around 1300, and since then it has been a royal castle, a fortress and a prison.

p62.caption: Victoria Terrasse
p62.fact: Pretty building, dark past: during the Second World War this was the Gestapo's headquarters in Oslo. These days, thankfully, it's home to Norway's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

p67.caption: The Birkebeiner statue
p67.story:
Back when I first started thinking about visiting Norway (my friend lives around here), I'd look up Lillehammer on Google Maps, and this statue was the picture that kept popping up. So seeing it in person was a bit surreal. It already felt familiar, as if I was connected to it through my friend.

It shows the Birkebeiners carrying the 18-month-old Prince Håkon Håkonsson, who grew up to be King Håkon IV.
p67.fact: The story goes that in 1206 two Birkebeiner skiers carried the baby prince across the mountains to safety. Norway still remembers it every year with the Birkebeiner ski race.

p69.story: We don't really have blueberries in India, so they always felt like an exotic fruit. After moving to the UK they became part of my usual diet. But seeing where they actually come from, and picking them myself, was a nice experience.

p70.caption: Leia
p70.story: This is Leia, my friend's dog, who quickly became a very good friend and my companion all across Jotunheimen. I kept covering her up with my hoodie or jacket, though honestly, I was a little jealous: she managed to look effortlessly cosy most of the time.

p71.caption: Norwegian tacos
p71.story: The full spread for 'Norwegian tacos', with Pepsi Max, of course. Not quite what I was expecting when my friend said tacos, but I can't complain.

p73.story: The boat ride across Gjende to start the Besseggen hike. It was the first time I'd seen water this bright blue-green. Ice-cold, of course, but I still wanted to jump in.

p79.caption: Kvikk Lunsj at the top
p79.story: I love that Kvikk Lunsj literally translates to 'quick lunch'. This was at the highest point of the trail, which felt like the right place for one.
p79.fact: Freia has been making it since 1937, and the wrapper even carries Norway's mountain code. A proper hiking snack.

p81.caption: The last shots of the Besseggen hike

p82.caption: Borgund Stave Church
p82.fact: Around 1180, so well over 800 years old and still standing. It's one of the best-preserved stave churches in Norway.

p84.caption: My first time in a kayak

p86.caption: Out on the Nærøyfjord
p86.fact: It's one of the narrowest fjords in the world, and a UNESCO World Heritage site.

p94.caption: Oslo City Hall
p94.fact: Every December, the Nobel Peace Prize is handed out in here.

p95.caption: A cabin we passed on the way

p99.caption: Hot dog, grilled on a stick over the fire

dayofreturn.title: Day of return
dayofreturn.intro: The drive back to the airport.

hytte.title: The hytte
hytte.intro: The hytte (cabin) where we stayed, between the hike and the fjords.

lillehammer.title: Lillehammer
lillehammer.intro: Just a stop of an hour or two on the drive from Oslo up to the Jotunheimen region. A quiet town with lovely people, and the place where I really came to appreciate the Norwegian accent.

settings.name: Aaditya
settings.title: Latitudes
settings.intro:
Hi! I'm Aaditya, but friends and family call me Aadi.

Four years ago I packed up, left India and moved to the UK to study, start over, and see as much of the world as my weekends allowed. Somewhere along the way the camera stopped being a thing I carried and became the way I see places. I'm the friend who stops mid-hike for one more shot.

I made this journal to give those photos a home (and because my friends were tired of me never posting anything online :P). It's a new project and it'll keep growing: these are the places I've wandered into so far, and the little stories behind the pictures.
